newsitem.title: JAPAN: Anti-smoke rules grow in cigarette-prone Asia.
newsitem.headline: Anti-smoke rules grow in cigarette-prone Asia.

text.p: An American cigarette company admission that smoking is addictive could keep on track laws pushing cigarette-prone Asians toward a smoke-free zone.

From Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto being sued for lighting up, to delegates who stubbed out cigarettes before this year's Chinese parliament, to tobacco manufacturers plans, Asia is less and less an official smokers haven.

But despite Asian advances towards snuffing out cigarettes, anti-smoking activists complain many countries only pay lip service to tobacco campaigns, worry teenagers do not hear the message, and fear manufacturers may target Asia as the once lucrative U.S. market declines.

The questioning has been set off by last Friday's admission by United States Liggett Group Inc. that smoking is addictive, and the firm's agreement to pay 25 percent of its pre-tax profits for the next quarter of a century to 22 U.S. states.
Liggett, maker of Chesterfield cigarettes, is the smallest of the major U.S. tobacco companies.
Despite a campaign to ban the habit, smoking is increasing in China at 2.0 percent a year, compared with developed world rates where smokers are falling by about 1.0 percent.

Deputies to China's parliament stubbed out cigarettes at this year's session of the National People's Congress after Premier Li Peng turned the cavernous Great Hall of the People into a no smoking zone.
Smoking is also officially banned on all Chinese airlines, ships, railways, buses, subways, taxis, and in waiting rooms.
Offenders risk fines of up to 50 yuan ($6.0) in a land where urban residents earn about 500 yuan a month.
In India, the world's second most populous nation, a New Delhi Federal Health Ministry spokesman said smoking was on the decline except among university students.
India is the world's third largest tobacco producer. About 85 per cent of its tobacco is consumed in the domestic market.
In Malaysia, an anti-tobacco consumers association in Penang said tobacco companies facing declining sales in the U.S would step up their sales efforts in Asia.
"We will become victims of dumping and double standards," the association said after the Liggett announcement.

In a sign that anti-smoking was a vote-getter in Asia in 1997, Pakistan's new Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif announced in his first address to the nation a complete ban on smoking in all government offices, trains and domestic flights.
Singapore and Australia still lead the way in Asia's toughest opposition to smoking. Both countries approach the issue with persuasion and prohibition.
In Singapore, smoking in public buildings, air-conditioned offices, shopping malls, bowling alleys, billiard halls, buses and taxis -- even while waiting in queues -- is banned.
Singapore's Environment Ministry caught 828 smokers in prohibited places in 1996, four times the 205 caught in 1995.

But the anti-smoking message appears to be struggling to get through -- particularly to the young. Singapore Health Ministry figures show 12.2 percent of 18 and 19 year olds were smoking in 1995 compared to 9.1 percent in 1984.
Overall, 17.4 percent of Singaporeans were smoking in 1995, compared to 20.0 percent in 1984.
Cigarette ads are banned in Australia, except at point of sale, and it has some of the world's toughest pack warnings.

Smoking regulations in Australia now prohibit the habit in public transport, theatres, cinemas, public buildings, federal airports, all flights by Australian airlines, public service offices and workplaces where there is flammable liquid.

In Japan, where Prime Minister Hashimoto, an admitted heavy smoker, was sued this month by five anti-smokers who said his habit violated the country's constitution, anti-smokers said the Liggett action was a victory for their cause.
"The news of Liggett was a great victory for anti-tobacco activists in the United States after a long, tough battle," said Nobuko Nakano, of the Women's Action on Smoking.
"I pay my respects to their guts, and their achievement. It is a great stimulus for Japanese activists".
